author: Antonialock
body:
this comes from annotation of cerevisiae sco1 and sco2 to Cell redox homeostasis from https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30593977/

the abstract says 
Members of the evolutionary conserved Sco protein family have been intensively studied regarding their role in the assembly of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase. However, experimental and structural data, specifically the presence of a thioredoxin-like fold, suggest that Sco proteins may also play a role in redox homeostasis

author: Antonialock
body:
with conclusions:

In summary, our data provide strong evidence that Sco proteins play a role in oxidative stress defense and redox homeostasis. Most likely, they are involved in ROS defense by reducing oxidized proteins in vivo via a thioredoxin-like function. Although some in vitro assays failed to show a thiol-oxidoreductase activity [[17]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6307045/#bib17), [[69]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6307045/#bib69), other studies provided evidence of such a function for prokaryotic Sco proteins [[19]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6307045/#bib19) and hSco2 [[15]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6307045/#bib15). In the latter case, the oxidoreductase activity seems to be essential for loading copper to hSco1 and hence for COX assembly [[30]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6307045/#bib30). Some Sco proteins might also possess a broader substrate spectrum and perform a thioredoxin/oxidoreductase function on other (artificially oxidized) proteins, especially under oxidative stress. Another possibility could be a function of Sco proteins, either directly by ROS scavenging or indirectly by acting as a mitochondrial redox signaling molecule as suggested for the hSco1 protein [[17]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6307045/#bib17). The question whether the antioxidant function of Sco proteins is direct or indirect and the possible interconnected mechanisms behind this function remain to be elucidated.
